cP:p0: This is the opening paragraph of Dickens's Preface to Bleak House (1853), in which he humorously recounts a Chancery judge's defense of the Court of Chancery, claiming its delays were due to public parsimony rather than systemic flaws. Dickens uses this anecdote ironically to set up his assertion that the novel's depiction of Chancery corruption is based on documented fact.
cP:p1: The author explains why he omitted a judge's joke about the Court of Chancery from the main narrative, noting it would have been more fitting placed in the dialogue of the character Conversation Kenge or Mr. Vholes, whom he suspects originated it.
cP:p2: This passage is from Dickens's preface to *Bleak House*, where he defends the authenticity of his satirical depiction of the Court of Chancery. He asserts that the fictional case of Jarndyce and Jarndyce and the character of Gridley are based on real instances of legal delay and excessive costs, providing specific contemporary examples from 1853 to substantiate his claims about the court's dysfunction and to critique public parsimony in funding judicial reform.
cP:p3: This is Dickens's preface to *Bleak House* addressing criticism of the novel's depiction of spontaneous combustion in Mr. Krook's death. Dickens defends the scientific plausibility of the phenomenon by citing historical cases and medical authorities, responding to objections from critic George Henry Lewes and asserting he thoroughly researched the subject before writing the novel.
cP:p4: This is Dickens's preface to Bleak House (1853), where he defends his depiction of the Court of Chancery and spontaneous combustion as factually grounded. This final statement summarizes his authorial approach: he has intentionally emphasized the romantic or extraordinary aspects of everyday, mundane subjects in the novel.
cP:p5: This is the date when Dickens wrote this preface to Bleak House, establishing the contemporaneous authenticity of his claims about the Court of Chancery's delays and the phenomenon of spontaneous combustion.

# Context

# Context for Chunk Situating

After Sir Leicester and Lady Dedlock return to Chesney Wold from Paris with a brilliant circle of distinguished guests, the narrator offers social commentary on the nature of the gathering. This passage discusses the presence of a modern, more insidious form of dandyism in the upper-class circle—one that extends beyond superficial fashion into matters of religion, aesthetics, and politics, representing a deeper moral and intellectual complacency rather than the harmless affectations of the Regency era under King George IV.
c12:p54: This chunk is part of a critical narrator's commentary on the guests assembled at Chesney Wold for a January house party. It follows a rhetorical question about what is "a little wrong" with the "brilliant and distinguished circle" despite their advantages, and it identifies a new form of dandyism—specifically religious dandyism—where fashionable guests adopt affected attitudes about faith and attempt to romanticize the lower classes through nostalgic rejection of modern progress.
c12:p55: This passage is part of Dickens's satirical critique of the "brilliant and distinguished circle" of fashionable society guests at Chesney Wold. It describes a second group of aristocratic visitors who maintain social artificiality by avoiding genuine emotion, suppressing reality, and resisting contemporary ideas and artistic innovation. This critique follows his earlier description of religious dandyism and precedes his mockery of politicians like Lord Boodle and William Buffy who obsess over ministerial appointments.

Using ridiculous rhyming names (Coodle, Doodle, Foodle, etc.), he illustrates the absurdity of aristocratic political maneuvering by arguing that the nation faces ruin simply because there is no suitable position available for the minor politician Noodle. The passage exemplifies Dickens's mockery of the self-absorbed political class and their disconnection from the actual concerns of the common people.

c16:p0: This opening passage introduces the restlessness of Lady Dedlock and establishes the contrasting domestic situation at Chesney Wold, where Sir Leicester is confined by gout while his wife moves constantly between her country estate and London townhouse. c16:p1: This passage follows the opening description of Lady Dedlock's restlessness and introduces Sir Leicester's affliction with gout. c16:p2: This passage describes Sir Leicester Dedlock's aristocratic acceptance of the family gout as an inherited affliction and mark of nobility. c16:p3: Sir Leicester Dedlock, afflicted with the family gout, lies resting in the great drawing-room at Chesney Wold surrounded by symbols of aristocratic dignity and ancestral power—his ancestors' portraits on the walls, the ancient oaks outside, and his wife's portrait nearby—all testifying to the grandeur and importance of the Dedlock name and lineage.

c31:p13: Charley recounts her encounter with Jenny, the brickmaker's wife, who came to the house searching for the narrator while she was away. Jenny mistook Charley for the narrator's maid, which delights Charley with a sense of importance and dignity in her role.
c31:p14: The narrator asks Charley to confirm whether Jenny, a poor brickmaker's wife whom the narrator once knew, actually mistook Charley for the narrator's maid when they encountered each other outside.
c31:p15: The narrator observes Charley's delight at being mistaken for her maid by Jenny, a poor woman they are about to visit. Charley takes pride in her role and appearance, displaying childish joy mixed with her attempts at mature dignity as a servant.
c31:p16: The narrator asks Charley where she saw Jenny, the brickmaker's wife, after Charley has mentioned that Jenny came looking for the narrator while she was away, hoping to get a glimpse of her.
c31:p17: Charley tells the narrator that she encountered Jenny, the brickmaker's wife, near the doctor's shop while wearing her black mourning dress. This is significant because it indicates someone in Jenny's household is ill or dying, requiring medicine from the doctor.
c31:p18: The narrator learns from Charley that Jenny, the brickmaker's wife, has returned to the neighborhood with her sister Liz. When the narrator expresses concern about Jenny's health, Charley explains that Jenny is actually caring for a sick boy—a destitute orphan who has wandered to Saint Albans. This revelation prompts the narrator's decision to visit Jenny's cottage to help the boy, leading to their encounter with Jo, a suffering vagrant who becomes central to the chapter's tragic events.
c31:p19: The narrator asks Charley whether Jenny, the brickmaker's wife, was obtaining medicine for a sick boy she found. This occurs during Charley's report about encountering Jenny and her sister Liz in town, who have returned to the neighborhood after being away. The boy in question is revealed to be Jo, a homeless child with fever symptoms who Charley and the narrator subsequently bring to their home.
c31:p20: The narrator (Esther) and Charley visit Jenny, a brickmaker's wife, who is caring for a sick boy named Jo. When Esther asks if Jenny is getting medicine for the boy, Charley explains that Jenny said the boy had once helped her in the past, so she is now returning the kindness by nursing him through his illness.
c31:p21: Charley has just informed the narrator that Jenny, a brickmaker's wife, has returned to the neighborhood and has been searching for the narrator. Jenny is caring for a sick boy who came from London and has been moved around by authorities. The narrator, reading Charley's eager expression and folded hands, decides they should visit Jenny's cottage to help the ill boy.
c31:p22: The narrator decides to visit Jenny, a brickmaker's wife, after Charley reports that Jenny came looking for her. They prepare to leave the house to check on a sick boy staying at Jenny's cottage. This chunk describes their departure.
c31:p23: The narrator and Charley travel to Jenny's cottage on a cold, stormy night to visit a sick boy. This passage describes the atmospheric weather and sky they observe as they journey through the countryside toward the brickmaker's dwelling, setting an ominous tone for their discovery of Jo, the ill vagrant boy sheltering there.
c31:p24: This passage occurs as Esther Summerson and her maid Charley walk toward Jenny's cottage on a cold, dark night to check on a sick boy. The chunk captures Esther's premonition of impending illness—a moment of uncanny self-awareness before she discovers that Charley is infected with smallpox, which Esther will subsequently contract while nursing her devoted servant back to health. The passage marks the threshold moment before Esther's life is transformed by illness and her eventual loss of sight.
c31:p25: The narrator and Charley arrive at the brickmaker's cottage to visit Jenny and find a sick boy named Jo who has come from London. This chunk describes their arrival at the miserable settlement where the kilns are operating.
c31:p26: The narrator and her maid Charley visit Jenny's cottage to help a sick boy named Jo who has recently arrived from London. Jenny, a brickmaker's wife, has taken him in out of pity, as he had once helped her. Jo is suffering from a fever and has nowhere to go. This passage describes their arrival at the cottage and their first glimpse of the boy's desperate condition.
c31:p27: The narrator (Esther Summerson) and her maid Charley visit Jenny, a brickmaker's wife, after learning that Jenny has been looking for them. Upon entering Jenny's cottage, they find a sick boy named Jo who reacts with fear and confusion when he sees the narrator, apparently mistaking her for someone else or believing she has come to take him to a burial ground.
c31:p28: The narrator and Charley visit Jenny's cottage to help a sick boy named Jo. When the narrator enters and lifts her veil, Jo reacts with sudden terror, believing she is a supernatural figure come to take him to the burial ground. The narrator stops in her tracks upon witnessing his frightened response.
c31:p29: Jo, a sick boy from Tom-all-Alone's in London, has been brought to Jenny's cottage by Esther Summerson and Charley. Delirious with fever, Jo mistakes Esther for another woman and fears she has come to take him to the burial ground, expressing his terror and refusal to go there.
c31:p30: The narrator and Charley visit Jenny, a brickmaker's wife, at her cottage to check on a sick boy named Jo. When they arrive, Jo reacts with terror to the narrator, mistaking her for another woman and raving about being taken to the burial ground. The narrator lifts her veil and speaks to Jenny, who reassures the delirious boy while trying to calm his fears.
c31:p31: The narrator and Charley visit Jenny, a brickmaker's wife, to check on a sick boy. When the narrator enters the cottage and lifts her veil, the delirious boy (Jo) becomes frightened, believing she has come to take him to the burial ground. He cries out in alarm, thinking he recognizes her as someone from his past.
c31:p32: The narrator and Charley visit Jenny, a brickmaker's wife, to help a sick boy. When the narrator lifts her veil and speaks to Jenny, the boy Jo becomes frightened and claims the narrator has come to take him to the burial ground. Jenny tries to calm him, saying "This is MY lady, Jo," to which Jo responds with confusion, asking "Who?" as he mistakes the narrator for another woman he fears.
c31:p33: Jo, a sick vagrant boy, mistakes the narrator for a woman he fears and refuses to be taken to the burial ground, believing she will bury him. He is fevered and delirious while sheltering in Jenny's cottage.
c31:p34: Jenny is reassuring Jo, a sick and delirious boy who has mistaken the narrator (Esther Summerson) for another woman. Jenny clarifies that Esther is her lady employer, not the mysterious "other one" Jo keeps referring to, as Jo has been confused and fearful throughout the day about being taken to the burial ground.
c31:p35: Jo, a delirious boy with a high fever, is being examined by Esther Summerson and Charley at Jenny's cottage. Despite being told the visitor is Jenny's lady, Jo insists that Esther resembles another woman he has previously encountered, confusing her identity as he struggles with illness and delirium.
c31:p36: The narrator and Charley visit Jenny, a brickmaker's wife, to help a desperately ill vagrant boy named Jo who has come from London. When they arrive at the cottage, Jo is terrified and delirious, confusing the narrator with another woman. Charley, with her experience nursing her sick father, compassionately tends to Jo by seating him in a chair and wrapping his rags around him, her young face reassuring him despite his confusion and fear.
c31:p37: The narrator and Charley visit Jenny, a brickmaker's wife, to check on a sick boy named Jo who has come from London. When they arrive, Jo becomes confused and frightened, mistaking the narrator for another woman. Here, Charley attempts to reassure Jo by confirming that the narrator is Jenny's lady, not the woman he fears.
c31:p38: Charley helps comfort a sick, delirious boy named Jo whom the narrator has brought home from a brickmaker's cottage. Despite Jo's confused fear of the narrator, Charley calmly tends to him, reassuring him about her mistress's identity while warming his ragged clothes as he shivers from fever.
c31:p39: The narrator and Charley bring a sick, delirious boy named Jo to their home. Jo confuses the narrator with another woman he knew, believing she has come to force him to the burial ground. When Charley reassures him that the narrator is actually her mistress, Jo expresses doubt, still thinking the narrator resembles "the t'other one." This line is Jo's resigned acceptance after Charley's denial.
c31:p40: The narrator (Esther Summerson) and her maid Charley visit a poor brick maker's cottage after learning that a sick boy named Jo has arrived there. Upon finding Jo delirious and shivering with fever, Esther offers to help him, asking what ails him. Jo responds that he is alternately freezing and burning, suffering from severe pain and confusion.
c31:p41: Jo, a sick vagrant boy, describes his symptoms of fever to Esther Summerson after she and Charley discover him ill at Jenny's cottage. His delirious state and descriptions of freezing and burning sensations indicate he is suffering from a serious illness, which will later prove contagious to Charley and Esther herself.
c31:p42: The narrator asks Jenny, the brickmaker's wife, when the sick boy (Jo) arrived at her cottage. This occurs after the narrator and Charley visit Jenny's home to check on a poor person in need, and they discover Jo, a destitute boy suffering from fever who has wandered from London.
c31:p43: The narrator and Charley visit Jenny, a brickmaker's wife, to inquire about a poor boy who has recently appeared in the neighborhood. Jenny explains that she found the boy, Jo, at the corner of town that morning and had previously known him from London, where he lived in Tom-all-Alone's. Jo is severely ill with fever and delirium, having recently arrived from London in a wretched condition.
c31:p44: The narrator and her maid Charley visit Jenny, a brickmaker's wife, and discover a severely ill boy named Jo. When asked where he came from in London, Jo responds that he came from Tom-all-Alone's, a notorious slum. This exchange occurs as the narrator tries to understand the boy's circumstances and origins before bringing him back to her home for shelter.
c31:p45: This chunk describes the boy Jo's delirious state during his illness at the cottage. After being found sick and brought to the cottage by Jenny, Jo exhibits symptoms of fever—alternating between chills and heat, confusion, and extreme weakness. The narrator observes his inability to maintain focus or awareness, which underscores the severity of his condition and the urgency of finding him proper medical care.
c31:p46: The narrator, visiting a brickmaker's cottage with her maid Charley, encounters a severely ill boy named Jo who has recently arrived from London. She asks this question while trying to understand his condition and circumstances.
c31:p47: Jo, a sick street boy from Tom-all-Alone's in London, has arrived at Jenny's cottage in the brickmaker's village. Esther and Charley visit to help, and Jo, fevered and confused, speaks about coming from London the previous day and being driven on by various people, unsure of where he is going.
c31:p48: The narrator asks where the sick boy Jo is going after he arrives at Jenny's cottage with a fever. Jo has wandered from London and speaks deliriously about being "moved on" repeatedly, claiming he is going "somewheres" but unable to specify a destination.
c31:p49: Jo, a destitute boy suffering from fever, has been brought to the protagonist's home after being found ill by Jenny, the brickmaker's wife. The narrator and Charley are trying to help him, but Jo is delirious and confused, speaking about being constantly moved along by authorities. In this passage, Jo explains his aimless wandering, mentioning that he was given money by "the t'other one" and has been harassed by Mrs. Snagsby and others to keep moving. He reveals he came from Tom-all-Alone's slum in London and took the Stolbuns Road without clear purpose or destination.
c31:p50: Jo, a sick and delirious boy found by the narrator and taken in, repeatedly speaks to Charley while rambling about his movements and persecution, always directing his remarks toward her rather than the narrator.
c31:p51: The narrator asks this question about Jo, a sick vagrant boy, after discovering his poor health and inability to care for himself. She is consulting with Jenny, the brickmaker's wife, about what steps can be taken to help the boy, who is suffering from a high fever and delirium after arriving from London.
c31:p52: Jenny, the brickmaker's wife, explains to the narrator why she cannot continue sheltering the sick boy Jo, despite her compassion. She describes the help she and Liz have already provided—food, medicine, and attempts to find him refuge—but fears her abusive husband's reaction if he discovers the boy. She anticipates Liz's return from seeking assistance at local institutions.
c31:p53: The narrator and Charley visit Jenny, a brickmaker's wife, to help a sick boy (Jo) they've learned about. When Jenny's friend Liz returns after unsuccessfully trying to find shelter for Jo at various institutions, the boy prepares to leave. Charley instinctively comforts Jenny's sick child, demonstrating her natural maternal care and connection to her own family responsibilities.
c31:p54: The narrator and Charley have brought the desperately ill boy Jo to Jenny's cottage. While they care for him, Liz (Jenny's friend) attempts to find him shelter in a proper refuge by going from one official to another, but is shuttled back and forth between bureaucratic offices that refuse to help. When she returns with news that both their masters are approaching and they can no longer hide the boy, Jenny and Liz give him a few coins, and he leaves the cottage. The passage critiques the callous inefficiency of poor relief institutions that evade their duties rather than fulfill them.
c31:p55: This passage occurs after the narrator and Charley visit Jenny's cottage to find a sick boy (Jo) who has come from London. The boy is suffering from fever and delirium. Liz, another poor woman who has been trying unsuccessfully to get the boy admitted to a refuge, returns to the cottage and reports that both her master and Jenny's master are approaching home. The women give Jo a few coins and hurry him out. This excerpt captures Liz's departure as she thanks Charley, says goodbye to Jenny, and rushes home to tend to her own child while anxiously watching for her drunken husband's return.
c31:p56: After Jenny and Liz fail to find institutional help for the sick boy Jo, they must leave him due to fear of their husbands' arrival. The narrator decides she and Charley must pursue Jo themselves to prevent his death, following him toward the brick-kiln where he plans to shelter among the warm bricks.
c31:p57: The narrator and Charley pursue the sick boy Jo into the rain after leaving Jenny's cottage. Despite his illness and the foul weather, Jo refuses shelter and attempts to continue wandering. The narrator tries to convince him to come with them for protection from the elements.
c31:p58: The narrator and Charley encounter a sick, delirious boy named Jo in Jenny's cottage. After finding him in poor condition, the narrator offers him shelter for the night, which he initially refuses, claiming he can sleep among the warm bricks.
c31:p59: The narrator and Charley encounter a sick boy named Jo who has fled from London. After finding him at Jenny's cottage suffering from fever, they bring him home and offer him shelter for the night. When they ask him to come inside, Jo refuses shelter, insisting he can sleep among the warm bricks of the kilns outside.
c31:p60: Charley tries to persuade Jo, a dying street boy they've taken in, not to sleep among the warm bricks of the kiln, warning him that people die there. Jo insists he can shelter himself there despite the danger.
c31:p61: Jo, a sick street boy taken in by the narrator, becomes delirious and confused about the narrator's identity. He believes she resembles another woman he knew and fears she has come to take him to the burial ground. In this moment, he expresses his grim observations about death being common everywhere, particularly in the slums, before asking Charley in confusion whether there are three different women.
c31:p62: The narrator and Charley encounter a delirious, fever-stricken boy named Jo at Jenny's cottage. When the narrator approaches him, Jo becomes frightened and confused, mistaking her for another woman. Both Charley and the narrator react with fear to his distressed behavior and wild staring.
c31:p63: The narrator and Charley convince the delirious street boy Jo to leave the brick-maker's cottage and return with them to their home for shelter and care, despite his initial resistance and confusion.
c31:p64: The narrator brings the sick boy Jo to her home for shelter. She leaves him in the hall while she goes to consult with her guardian about what to do with him. She discovers Mr. Skimpole has unexpectedly arrived and is present in the drawing-room.
c31:p65: The narrator brings the sick boy Jo to her home and presents him to her guardian for assessment. The servants gather to witness the boy's arrival, where he sits shivering in the window-seat with Charley attending to him, appearing as pitiful as a wounded animal.
c31:p66: The narrator and Charley bring a sick boy (Jo) to their home after finding him ill at Jenny's cottage. The guardian examines Jo and seeks Mr. Skimpole's opinion on what should be done with the fevered, delirious child.
c31:p67: Mr. Skimpole advises the narrator's guardian to turn out Jo, a sick and destitute boy whom they have taken in from the streets, suggesting he be expelled rather than cared for due to fears about contagion from his fever.
c31:p68: The narrator's guardian questions Mr. Skimpole's callous suggestion to turn out the sick boy Jo into the cold night, objecting to Skimpole's recommendation that they simply give the dying child money and send him away rather than provide shelter and care.
c31:p69: Mr. Skimpole, a visitor to the house, objects to sheltering Jo, a desperately ill vagrant boy whom the narrator and Charley have brought home. Despite the boy's critical condition with fever, Skimpole argues for turning him out, claiming he has a constitutional aversion to illness and that the boy poses a health risk.
c31:p70: Mr. Skimpole, an irresponsible and callous guest, retreats to the drawing-room after callously suggesting that Jo, a desperately ill and delirious boy whom the narrator and Charley have brought to the house for shelter, should be turned out onto the street. He offers this cruel advice in a casual, detached manner while seated at the music-stool, indifferent to the boy's suffering from a serious fever.
c31:p71: Mr. Skimpole argues callously for turning out the sick boy Jo, claiming his childish nature exempts him from moral responsibility. He suggests dismissing Jo with monetary compensation rather than providing shelter and care, exemplifying his selfish indifference to the suffering poor while the narrator and her guardian seek to help the fevered, homeless boy.
c31:p72: The narrator and her guardian have brought a sick, delirious boy (Jo) into their home for shelter. Mr. Skimpole has suggested turning the boy out, arguing he would be no worse off than before. The guardian questions what the boy should do if cast out, challenging Skimpole's callous suggestion.
c31:p73: Mr. Skimpole dismisses the guardian's concern about what will happen to the sick boy Jo if turned out onto the street, expressing his characteristic indifference to practical consequences and social responsibility.
c31:p74: The narrator and Charley discover a sick, malnourished boy named Jo at Jenny's cottage. After bringing him to their home, the narrator's guardian expresses outrage at the systemic injustice that a destitute vagrant child has no access to hospital care, while a convicted criminal would be guaranteed such treatment. This moment reflects the novel's critique of Victorian social institutions that fail the poor.
c31:p75: Mr. Skimpole questions why the sick boy Jo should not simply be made a prisoner, so that he could receive proper hospital care and shelter. This occurs during a conversation where Skimpole callously suggests turning the boy out into the street, while the narrator's guardian expresses moral outrage at the failure of official institutions to help the destitute child.
c31:p76: Mr. Jarndyce reacts with frustration to Mr. Skimpole's callous suggestion that the sick boy Jo should be turned out into the street, finding Skimpole's reasoning both amusing and infuriating.
c31:p77: Mr. Skimpole argues that the sick boy Jo should be turned out of the house because he has a dangerous fever. When challenged about this callous position, Skimpole suggests it would be more "poetic" and "respectable" if the boy had committed a crime to get into prison, where he would receive proper care, rather than being a mere vagrant.
c31:p78: The narrator's guardian criticizes Mr. Skimpole's callous indifference to the dying boy Jo by sarcastically remarking that there is no one else on earth quite like him. This occurs during a heated discussion where Skimpole advocates turning the sick boy out onto the streets, while the guardian argues that a convicted prisoner would receive better care in a hospital than this innocent suffering child.
c31:p79: Mr. Skimpole, a morally indifferent character who has just visited the house, argues in defense of the sick boy Jo's potential criminality. When challenged about why Jo should not be turned out onto the street despite his severe fever, Skimpole cynically suggests that Jo would be more "poetic" and interesting if he were a criminal stealing bread out of hunger rather than merely a poor vagabond. His rhetorical speech justifies petty theft as a form of "misdirected energy" with romantic appeal, revealing his callous selfishness and lack of compassion for the suffering boy's plight.
c31:p80: The narrator observes that the sick boy Jo is deteriorating in health while Mr. Skimpole argues that Jo should be turned out of the house, dismissing concerns about his severe fever and deteriorating condition.
c31:p81: Mr. Skimpole suggests turning out a sick boy (Jo) who has been brought to the house, arguing that the boy is getting worse and poses a health risk. This occurs after the narrator and Charley bring Jo, a fevered street boy, to shelter at their home, and Skimpole expresses his constitutional objection to harboring someone with a "very bad sort of fever."
c31:p82: Mr. Skimpole's callous suggestion that Jo be turned out onto the street despite his dangerous illness, shown with an amiable expression that masks his indifference to human suffering.
c31:p83: The narrator and Charley have brought Jo, a sick and delirious boy from Tom-all-Alone's, to the guardian's home seeking shelter. Mr. Skimpole callously suggests turning the boy out, but the guardian decides to keep Jo overnight in the loft-room by the stable until morning, when he can arrange proper admission to a hospital or refuge, despite the poor state of the system that makes such intervention necessary.
c31:p84: After the narrator and her guardian decide to shelter the sick boy Jo in the loft-room for the night despite Mr. Skimpole's objections, Mr. Skimpole calls out to them as they leave the drawing-room to return to the boy, asking if they are going back to see him.
c31:p85: Mr. Jarndyce agrees to go back to check on the ill boy Jo in the loft-room, despite Mr. Skimpole's objections to helping the sick vagrant.
c31:p86: Mr. Skimpole, after callously suggesting the sick boy Jo be turned out into the street, envies Mr. Jarndyce and Miss Summerson (the narrator) for their willingness to help others and their strong constitutions, claiming he himself lacks the will to do anything uncomfortable or unpleasant.
c31:p87: The narrator and Charley have brought the sick, delirious boy Jo into the household for shelter. The guardian decides to keep him in the loft-room overnight, but Mr. Skimpole callously suggests turning the boy out. As they prepare to leave Jo, the guardian asks Skimpole if he can offer any medical recommendations, speaking with barely restrained anger at Skimpole's heartlessness.
c31:p88: Mr. Skimpole offers minimal medical advice for the sick boy Jo after being asked by Mr. Jarndyce what he might recommend, while characteristically deflecting responsibility and complimenting Miss Summerson's practical abilities instead of genuinely helping.
c31:p89: This passage describes the household's efforts to shelter Jo, the sick street boy, after Esther and Charley bring him home from the brickmaker's cottage. The guardians and servants prepare a loft-room for him, provide care and comfort, and arrange for a letter to be sent in the morning to secure his admission to proper medical facilities. The passage emphasizes the kindness shown to Jo despite Mr. Skimpole's earlier callous objections to harboring him.
c31:p90: After Jo is brought to the house suffering from fever, the narrator and her guardian tend to him while Mr. Skimpole remains detached. While Ada stays in their room with a cold and the servants care for Jo in the loft-room, Mr. Skimpole amuses himself at the piano, later returning to entertain them with a sentimental ballad about a peasant boy inspired by Jo's plight.
c31:p91: Mr. Skimpole sings a ballad about a peasant boy that he claims always makes him cry, demonstrating his emotional theatricality while the household tends to the sick boy Jo.
c31:p92: This passage occurs at the end of the evening after Jo, a sick and delirious boy from Tom-all-Alone's, has been taken in by the household. Mr. Skimpole, having earlier callously suggested turning the boy out onto the street, now entertains the company with cheerful toasts and fanciful speculation about Jo's future, displaying his characteristic self-centered charm and moral indifference while the narrator and her guardian show genuine concern for the boy's welfare.
c31:p93: The narrator provides shelter for a sick, delirious boy named Jo who was found wandering in poor health after being turned away from various refuges. After settling him in a loft-room for the night, the narrator goes to bed relieved that he is now safe and cared for, unaware that he will disappear by morning.
c31:p94: The narrator wakes to unusual activity in the house early in the morning after Jo, a sick boy from the slums, was placed in the loft-room overnight for shelter. She checks whether something is amiss, noticing the lantern still burning in the loft-window where Jo was left to rest.
c31:p95: The boy Jo has mysteriously disappeared from the loft-room where he was being sheltered overnight due to his severe fever. The narrator wakes to unusual activity before daybreak and asks a servant if anything is wrong. The servant's cryptic response indicates Jo is gone.
c31:p96: The narrator is asking a servant in the early morning about the condition of Jo, a sick boy they had taken in the night before. Jo has mysteriously disappeared from the loft-room where they left him to recover.
c31:p97: The boy Jo, who was taken in ill and sheltered in the loft-room overnight, has disappeared during the night. When the narrator checks on him at daybreak, she learns from one of the servants that he has vanished without trace, despite the locked door and closed trap.
c31:p98: When the narrator awakes at daybreak to discover the sick boy (Jo) has vanished from the loft-room where he was sheltered overnight, a servant reports that the boy is gone. The narrator initially asks if he is worse, to which the servant replies "Gone, miss," prompting the narrator's shocked response: "Dead!"
c31:p99: The narrator discovers that Jo, a sick boy she and Charley brought to shelter in the loft-room overnight, has mysteriously disappeared by morning. When asked if he is worse, a servant reports that Jo has vanished without trace, despite the door remaining locked and the lantern still burning.
c31:p100: Jo, a sickly vagrant boy, disappeared overnight from the loft-room where he had been sheltered at the narrator's guardian's house. The household discovered his absence the next morning and struggled to understand how he escaped, since the door remained locked and nothing was missing. While the family believed he had wandered away in a delirious state, Mr. Skimpole callously suggested the boy had deliberately left out of politeness, considering himself a safety hazard due to his fever.
c31:p101: This passage describes the frantic search for Jo, the sick street boy, after he mysteriously disappears during the night from the loft-room where he had been taken in and sheltered. It follows the discovery of his absence at daybreak and precedes the five-day search effort, after which the narrator's attention turns to Charley's sudden illness from fever.
c31:p102: The narrator has been searching for Jo, a sick homeless boy she and Charley sheltered in a loft room overnight. Despite precautions, he disappeared mysteriously before dawn. After five days of fruitless searching through the brick-kilns, cottages, and surrounding area with no trace found, the narrator's attention shifts when Charley falls gravely ill with fever, marking the beginning of her own battle with the contagion Jo carried.
c31:p103: Jo, a sick boy found at the brickmaker's cottage, has mysteriously vanished from the loft-room where he was sheltered for the night. After five days of fruitless searching, Charley—the narrator's young maid—begins to exhibit signs of illness, which marks the beginning of her contraction of the fever that Jo carried.
c31:p104: The narrator asks Charley if she is cold after noticing her maid shivering at the table while writing in the evening. This moment marks the beginning of Charley's illness with the fever that will soon affect the narrator as well, following Jo the crossing-sweeper's unexplained disappearance from the loft-room where he had been sheltered.
c31:p105: Charley begins showing symptoms of illness while working at her writing desk in the narrator's room. The narrator realizes Charley is shivering and trembling, and Charley reveals she has been feeling unwell since the previous day at the same time. This marks the onset of the illness that will confine both Charley and later the narrator to her room for an extended period.
c31:p106: The narrator has discovered that Charley is becoming ill with a fever. Realizing the illness is contagious, she locks the door between her room and the shared sitting-room to prevent Ada from entering and risking infection, even as Ada arrives and knocks at the door.
c31:p107: The narrator Esther discovers that her maid Charley has contracted a serious illness after nursing the sick boy Jo. Realizing she has been exposed to contagion, Esther locks herself away from her ward Ada to prevent transmitting the disease to her. This passage marks the moment Esther first isolates herself from Ada, beginning a prolonged separation that will last through her own subsequent illness and blindness.
c31:p108: This passage describes the narrator's response to Charley's illness from the fever contracted while nursing the sick boy Jo. After Charley falls gravely ill, the narrator isolates herself to prevent spreading the contagion to Ada, her beloved companion. Though Ada repeatedly comes to the door and window seeking contact, the narrator maintains distance while tenderly communicating through barriers, foreshadowing her own imminent illness and blindness.
c31:p109: Esther Summerson, the narrator, describes her isolation and precautions after contracting the same illness as her maid Charley. She explains how she has reorganized her living quarters to maintain separation from her friend Ada, employing a single trusted servant to attend to her needs and facilitate her limited outdoor activities with her guardian while avoiding contact with Ada.
c31:p110: Esther Summerson describes Charley's severe illness from the contagion she caught while nursing Jo, a sick vagrant boy. Esther has isolated herself to prevent spreading the disease to Ada. During Charley's dangerous illness, Esther sits vigil by her bedside, moved by the child's remarkable patience and fortitude despite her suffering, finding spiritual instruction in her gentle endurance.
c31:p111: Esther Summerson nurses the seriously ill Charley, who contracted fever while caring for Jo, a sick boy brought to their home. As Charley's condition worsens and she deliriously recalls her responsibilities caring for her younger siblings after their father's death, Esther grieves over the possibility of losing her devoted young maid and worries about how to inform Charley's younger siblings of her potential death.
c31:p112: The narrator sits by Charley's bedside during the girl's dangerous illness from scarlet fever. During lucid moments, Charley speaks of her love for her siblings Tom and Emma, recalls biblical stories of resurrection she had read to comfort her dying father, and expresses her faith that even if she dies, Tom might pray for her restoration as she once prayed for their father's. The narrator responds by offering spiritual comfort, explaining that these biblical resurrections teach hope for heavenly restoration.
c31:p113: The narrator is reflecting on Charley's illness and recovery. During her extended care of the fevered Charley, the narrator witnesses the child's unwavering gentleness and patience despite delirium and suffering. This passage emphasizes Charley's spiritual fortitude, recalling her late father's faith in divine salvation even in his poverty and despair.
c31:p114: Charley recovers from a severe smallpox-like illness after weeks of critical condition, during which the narrator nursed her while keeping Ada isolated to prevent contagion. c58:p2:
# Context

This passage depicts how rumors of Lady Dedlock's disappearance and scandalous separation from Sir Leicester spread through London's fashionable society. Dickens satirizes the shallow nature of London's upper classes and merchants, showing how gossip becomes fashionable commodity through manipulative social networks. Shop owners and society figures deliberately cultivate and exploit the scandal to maintain influence over the "flock" of fashionable people who blindly follow their lead. The scene contrasts sharply with the domestic tragedy unfolding at the Dedlock townhouse, where Sir Leicester lies ill, desperately waiting for his wife's return.
c58:p3: This passage continues the satirical portrayal of London gossip surrounding Lady Dedlock's disappearance. It demonstrates how rumor spreads through fashionable society, showing a witty remark made by a society figure that reduces Lady Dedlock's scandal to sporting terminology, mocking both the gossip-mongers and the trivial nature of their commentary.

The chunk describes how people of lower social standing, who know nothing about Lady Dedlock, nonetheless pretend to discuss her as a topic of their own in order to appear fashionable and maintain their social reputation. The passage extends the earlier theme (from [P2]-[P4]) of how rumors and gossip about Lady Dedlock spread through different social circles—from jewelers and mercers to the librarian Sladdery's "high connexion" to Parliament itself. The narrator's tone remains bitterly ironic, mocking the pretentious and derivative nature of secondhand social discourse among those seeking to appear cultured and informed.

c66:p9: This passage describes Volumnia's subjective experience of life at Chesney Wold during its decline. It portrays the grand but decaying estate as a melancholic, oppressive space filled with eerie echoes and emptiness, emphasizing the isolation and psychological toll of residing in the abandoned manor house.
c66:p10: This concluding paragraph summarizes the decline of Chesney Wold estate following Lady Dedlock's death and Sir Leicester's illness. It marks the end of the chapter by emphasizing the mansion's transformation from a grand, vibrant family seat into a dark, empty, lifeless shell, symbolizing the loss of passion and pride that once defined the Dedlock household.
c67:p0: This is the opening passage of the final chapter, in which Esther Summerson reflects on seven years of happiness as mistress of Bleak House and prepares to conclude her narrative account to an unknown reader.
c67:p1: This passage describes the birth of Ada's son following the death of her husband Richard. The narrator (Esther) recounts holding the newborn and how she, her own husband, and their guardian named the child after his deceased father, establishing the emotional and familial continuity that characterizes the chapter's reflection on seven years of domestic happiness at Bleak House.
c67:p2: This passage reflects on the birth and healing power of Ada's child. The baby, named after Ada's deceased husband Richard, arrives after his father's death. Though born for a different purpose than expected, the infant's presence profoundly restores Ada's emotional and spiritual wellbeing, awakening the narrator's deeper faith in divine goodness.
c67:p3: This passage concludes the narrator Esther's account of Ada's recovery and motherhood following her husband Richard's death. After describing how Ada's newborn son brought her healing and renewed hope, Esther reflects on witnessing Ada flourish in the garden with her child, marking Esther's own happiness at this time of restored contentment for those she loves.
c67:p4: Ada has recovered from her grief over Richard's death and has been living in the country with her newborn son. Her guardian now visits and asks when she will return to Bleak House, offering both his and the narrator's home as hers.
c67:p5: The narrator's guardian invites Ada to return to Bleak House as her permanent home once she and her infant son are fully recovered from childbirth, establishing the older estate as their primary residence.
c67:p6: This passage establishes the formal relationship between Ada and her guardian, explaining why she addresses him as "guardian" rather than by his given name. It occurs in the context of the narrator (Esther) reflecting on the seven years of happiness she has experienced at Bleak House, following Ada's recovery and the birth of her son. The chunk also reveals that Esther herself now has two daughters, marking the fulfillment of family life that has followed the resolution of the novel's central conflicts.
c67:p7: This passage appears in the final chapter of Bleak House, where Esther Summerson reflects on the seven years she has been mistress of Bleak House. She is describing the fates of her former servants and acquaintances, particularly Charley and her family (Emma and Tom), who have prospered in the years since the main events of the novel. Charley has married a prosperous miller in the neighborhood, while her siblings have grown up, with Tom now apprenticed to the miller. This is part of Esther's epilogue-like summary of how various characters have fared after the resolution of the novel's main plot.
c67:p8: This passage describes Caddy Jellyby's life seven years after the main events of the novel. It details her contentment in marriage to a lame but excellent husband, her dedicated motherhood to a deaf and dumb daughter, her modest prosperity, and her mother Mrs. Jellyby's disappointed reaction to what she considers an ignoble match, contrasting with Mrs. Jellyby's continued pursuit of charitable causes like women's parliamentary rights.
c67:p9: This passage is from the epilogue of Bleak House, where Esther Summerson reflects on the fates of various characters seven years after the main events. Here, she updates the reader on Caddy Jellyby's circle, specifically mentioning Peepy's career advancement at the Custom House and old Mr. Turveydrop's continued vanity and support of Peepy, including an ironic bequest of a clock that isn't rightfully his to give.
c67:p10: This passage occurs in the closing epilogue of *Bleak House*, where Esther Summerson reflects on her life seven years after the main events of the novel. She describes the domestic happiness she has found with her husband Allan Woodcourt and their children, while also recounting the fates of other characters. This particular chunk describes how Esther and her family used their savings to build a special room ("growlery") in their home as a gift for their beloved guardian, Mr. Jarndyce, demonstrating the deep affection and gratitude they feel toward him.
c67:p11: This passage appears near the end of the novel's epilogue, where Esther Summerson reflects on her life seven years after becoming mistress of Bleak House. She describes her enduring relationship with her guardian, Mr. Jarndyce, expressing her deep love and reverence for him while maintaining their familiar, comfortable dynamic. The passage emphasizes how their bond has remained unchanged despite the passage of time and life's trials, with Esther continuing to use her old nicknames and sit in her customary place beside him.
c67:p12: This passage reflects on a symbolic transformation in Esther's life. The "east wind" is a recurring motif throughout Bleak House representing disease, misery, and moral corruption. Esther's observation that the wind has never blown from the east since her guardian took her to read the nameplate at Bleak House's porch marks a spiritual and emotional turning point—suggesting that darkness and suffering have permanently lifted from her life. Her guardian's confirmation of this shift underscores how his presence has brought healing and redemption to her world.
c67:p13: This passage appears near the end of the chapter, as the narrator (Esther) reflects on the lasting effects of past sorrows on those she loves. It follows her descriptions of how various characters have fared in the seven years since becoming mistress of Bleak House, and precedes her tender reflections on her husband Allan and her enduring contentment with her life.
c67:p14: This passage reflects the narrator Esther's deep maternal bond with her young son Richard, who was born to Ada (Esther's beloved friend) and her late husband. Despite being his biological aunt, Esther has served as a second mother figure to the child, and he affectionately refers to her as one of his two mothers, demonstrating the close family relationships and love that have developed in the seven years since Esther became mistress of Bleak House.
c67:p15: This passage is Esther Summerson's reflection on the spiritual and moral wealth of her life with her husband Allan Woodcourt, a compassionate doctor. She emphasizes that true richness lies not in financial abundance but in the goodness and healing her husband brings to others through his medical practice and care for the suffering. This comes near the end of the novel's final chapter as Esther looks back contentedly on her seven years as mistress of Bleak House, celebrating how her husband is beloved and blessed by the people he serves.
c67:p16: Esther reflects on her life as a doctor's wife, acknowledging that the people's affection and praise are directed at her through her husband Allan's reputation and medical work, rather than for herself alone. She expresses her devotion to him and credits him entirely for any esteem she receives in their community.
c67:p17: This passage concludes the final chapter of *Bleak House*, where Esther Summerson, now married to Dr. Allan Woodcourt, reflects on her seven years as mistress of Bleak House. She is contentedly waiting for a visit from Ada, her guardian John Jarndyce, and young Richard, when Allan returns home and finds her sitting in the porch—the very place where Jarndyce once revealed her name to her years before. This moment captures the domestic happiness and fulfillment that Esther has achieved after the novel's tumultuous events.
c67:p18: The narrator, now happily married to Allan for seven years as mistress of Bleak House, sits in the porch on a moonlit night reflecting on her past appearance. When Allan arrives home and finds her there, he asks what she has been thinking about.
c67:p19: The narrator Esther reflects on her past appearance after smallpox scarred her face. While sitting in the porch with her husband Allan, she admits she has been thinking about how her lost beauty no longer matters to him, expressing gratitude that he loves her despite the physical changes wrought by her illness years ago.
c67:p20: The narrator Esther has been sitting in the porch at night, reflecting on her lost beauty from a past illness. Her husband Allan arrives home and asks what she's been thinking about. She admits she's been thinking about her old looks, and Allan playfully responds by calling her "my busy bee" and asking what thoughts she has about her former appearance.
c67:p21: Esther Summerson reflects on her lost beauty while sitting in the porch with her husband Allan, expressing that his love for her would not have been greater even if she had retained her former appearance before her illness disfigured her face.
c67:p22: Esther's reflective closing to Bleak House, where she sits in the porch at night thinking about her lost beauty. Her husband Allan teases her gently about her self-deprecating remarks regarding her appearance, which she lost to illness years before.
c67:p23: The narrator, Esther, is sitting in the porch with her husband Allan on a moonlit night. When asked what she's been thinking about, she admits she's been reflecting on her lost beauty from a severe illness earlier in the story. Allan playfully questions her, asking if she ever looks in the glass and suggesting she's prettier than ever. Esther confirms her earlier statement about her former looks with this phrase.
c67:p24: The narrator, now married to Allan (a doctor) and living contentedly at Bleak House, reflects on her life seven years later. In this scene, she sits with Allan in the porch at night, thinking about her lost beauty from a past illness. Allan gently teases her about her appearance, suggesting she is still beautiful.
c67:p25: The narrator reflects on her past appearance after becoming disfigured by illness, conversing with her husband Allan about whether she has become less beautiful. He asks if she ever looks in the glass, and she responds that he witnesses her doing so regularly.
c67:p26: The narrator Esther reflects on her lost beauty from smallpox scarring. Her husband Allan reassures her that she is actually prettier than she ever was, countering her insecurity about her changed appearance.
c67:p27: This is the final passage of the chapter, where Esther concludes her reflection on her appearance. After Allan asks if she realizes she is prettier than ever, Esther responds with characteristic humility, deflecting attention from herself to praise the beauty and virtue of her beloved family—her children, Ada, her husband, and her guardian—while humbly downplaying her own looks.
F2:p0: This passage is not from Bleak House by Charles Dickens. It appears to be from a 19th-century medical or scientific text describing a specific case study of a German liquor shopkeeper and drunkard in Columbus, USA, as documented by a dentist. It does not belong in Bleak House.
